newsitem.title: UK: UK repo traders hopeful about new money mkt regime.
newsitem.headline: UK repo traders hopeful about new money mkt regime.

text.p: Britain's money and gilt repo markets adjusted seamlessly to a new regime early this week and traders are confident that some of the wrinkles of the old system may have been ironed out for good.
On Monday, the Bank of England ended more than a century of tradition by terminating its exclusive money market relationship with London's discount houses.
It will now deal with a wider number of market participants, including banks, building societies and securities firms, and has introduced gilt repos into daily money market operations.
"It was a nice, steady first day with money market rates trading in a very narrow band," one gilt repo trader said.
Overnight money market rates never strayed above six percent on Monday, hovering for most of the session around 5-7/8, 5-3/4 percent -- exactly where they started out again on Tuesday.

Admittedly, Monday's money market shortage of 650 million stg was modest by any standards and was never likely to squeeze money market rates through the roof. But the repo trader said the Bank should be better equipped to cope with large market shortages under the new regime.
"The main thing is that more people can participate directly. The Bank will have a much clearer idea of how much money people are looking for in the cash market."
And because there are more players, liquidity will improve.
The reforms deprive the discount houses of their exclusive right to rediscount short-term bills -- effectively IOUs issued by companies and guaranteed by banks -- with the central bank.
There were only six discount houses operating in London and one of those -- Union Plc -- said last week it would no longer be a money market counterparty to the Bank of England.

Ian Perkins, director of the Gerrard Group and chairman of discount house Gerrard and King, said that under the old system "the total pile of bills was probably not big enough to deal with daily shortages."
As a result, a large daily shortage could force money rates up to prohibitive levels as the Bank scrambled to remove it.

The repo trader pointed out another advantage of the new regime -- because the Bank of England will be offering repos that expire in two weeks' time, rather than just overnight money, it should find it easier to iron out market fluctuations in the shape of large shortages.
The gilt repo market was set up just over a year ago, partly in order to attract more investors from abroad.

A repo, or repurchase agreement, involves the loan of a gilt stock to another party for a set period of time. As a result, the market can become much more liquid as investors can effectively short it without going through market makers.

General collateral rates, the market rates at which gilts are lent out, closely follow money market rates. The fact that the Bank is now using repos in its daily operations will give the market more credibility.

Of course this could sound a death knell for the discount houses, now deprived of their cosy relationship with the Bank of England. "Union Plc could be the shape of things to come for the remaining few," the repo trader said.
But other money market veterans said Union was the exception rather than the rule, and they added it was highly unlikely the other five remaining discount houses would follow suit.
Most discount houses have already diversified into other areas such as the repo money, proprietary trading, bond lending and equity stock lending.
